why.why: It works by reframing burnout not as a vague state but as a set of specific, detectable 'signals,' providing viewers with a practical mental checklist that increases watch time and shareability.

why.title: The Moon Isn’t Getting Bigger. Your Brain Is Tricking You.
why.why: This leverages the 'perceptual illusion' hook, a classic public-domain psychology trope, to immediately validate the viewer's curiosity and provide a quick, satisfying 'aha' moment that encourages completion.

hook_patterns: Direct physiological warning: 'Your body is screaming for you to stop...'
The invisible enemy: 'You have a cognitive bias that is costing you money/time.'
The perceptual lie: 'The object you are looking at is not what it seems.'
todays_angle: Focus on 'Invisible Self-Sabotage' by using public-domain concepts (like William James' 'Habit' or Maslow's 'Deficit') to explain why the viewer's brain actively resists their own goals.

ideas.title: The 'Habit' Trap (1908)
ideas.concept: Explain William James' concept that habits are the 'flywheel of society.' Show how a 10-second neural loop creates a 'groove' that makes quitting feel physically painful, not just mentally difficult.

ideas.title: The Maslow Deficit
ideas.concept: Use Maslow's Hierarchy to show why someone can't focus on 'growth' (top of pyramid) when their 'safety' or 'belonging' needs are quietly unmet. Frame it as 'Why your brain prioritizes survival over success.'

ideas.title: The Illusion of Choice
ideas.concept: Reference classic public-domain studies on priming or framing. Show how a subtle change in question wording changes the brain's 'default' answer, proving that 'choice' is often just a perception.

avoid: Generic '7 Brain Facts' listicles that lack a specific emotional hook or narrative arc.
Clickbaity 'Hungry Animal' or 'Mystery Object' hooks that have no direct relevance to human psychological mechanics.
